Years 11–13 Science

Learning expectations
Through Science, students explore fundamental scientific concepts through the disciplines of
biology, chemistry, physics, Earth and space science, and agricultural and horticultural science.
They are taught how to explain phenomena using evidence, scientific reasoning, data, and
disciplinary knowledge.

The learning area supports students to think critically, evaluate evidence, communicate scientific
understanding precisely, and apply disciplinary knowledge to develop evidence-based
explanations.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•    Clear progression from Years 9–10 through to specialist Years 12–13 science subjects and
     advanced science pathways.
•    Clear distinction between disciplinary knowledge and practices, supporting students to
     develop both deep scientific understanding and the ability to apply that understanding in
     different contexts.
•    Strong emphasis on scientific investigation, with students using a range of methods to gather
     and evaluate evidence, identify patterns and relationships, test ideas, and develop evidence-
     based explanations.
•    Greater visibility of scientific reasoning and applying scientific knowledge in practical contexts.
•    Explicit teaching of disciplinary writing, helping students explain, justify, evaluate, and
     communicate scientific understanding.
•    Strong connections between scientific knowledge and authentic real-world contexts, including
     health, sustainability, primary industries, engineering, technology, environmental
     management, and scientific research.


Subjects
Subjects within the Science learning area are:

•    Year 11 Science
•    Years 12–13 Agricultural and Horticultural Science
•    Years 12–13 Biology
•    Years 12–13 Chemistry
•    Years 12–13 Earth and Space Science
•    Years 12–13 Physics.

Learning and pathways

Year 11 Science
In Science, students are taught fundamental concepts of physical and biological sciences,
including matter, energy, environmental processes, and the interactions that shape the natural
world. They are taught how biological systems function and sustain life, and how to investigate
phenomena, gather evidence, and test theories.

Strands
Year 11 Science is organised into three strands:
•    Physical Science
•    Biological Science
•    Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design
•    Schools teach all knowledge and practices within the Year 11 Science curriculum and can
     determine how learning is organised across the year. Programmes may be taught linearly or
     may integrate content from the Physical Science and Biological Science strands where it
     supports meaningful connections between ideas. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary
     writing within subject-specific teaching to develop students’ proficiency in scientific
     communication.
•    The Year 11 programme is required to include opportunities for students to undertake both
     practical learning activities and scientific investigations, working independently and
     collaboratively. Together, these experiences support students to develop scientific knowledge,
     practical skills, and the ability to gather, analyse, and evaluate evidence.
•    Practicals may be short in duration and completed within part of a lesson. Scientific
     investigation explores questions or phenomena in greater depth and may be completed over
     one to two lessons.
•    Schools are required to provide opportunities for students to undertake:
     o   at least one investigation from five options provided within the curriculum teaching
         sequence
     o   at least two additional investigations, selected from either:
     o   the five options provided within the curriculum teaching sequence
     o   example investigations provided within the curriculum teaching sequence
     o   schools may develop their own investigations provided they align with the disciplinary
         knowledge and practices within the curriculum.
•    All investigations can be adapted to the local context, student interests, and available
     resources.
•    Knowledge and practices required to plan and conduct scientific investigations is provided at
     the end of the curriculum document. When designing a programme, schools select the
     appropriate knowledge and practices aligned with the methods and skills required to carry out
     the selected or developed investigation. These may be taught independently or integrated
     within and across the teaching programme.

Science supports learning across science-related disciplines and contributes to pathways into
health sciences, engineering, environmental management, agriculture and horticulture, technology,
biomedical science, energy systems, scientific research, and related disciplines.

Years 12–13 Agricultural and Horticultural Science
Students are taught to apply and extend knowledge of biological, environmental, physical,
technological, and management systems. They investigate how plant, animal, soil, environmental,
and production systems interact, and how management decisions influence productivity,
profitability, sustainability, and environmental outcomes. Students use scientific knowledge,
observations, data, and evidence to explain production outcomes, evaluate management practices,
and solve problems within agricultural and horticultural contexts.

Strands

Years 12–13 Agricultural and Horticultural Science strands are organised separately for each year
level.

Year 12 Agricultural and Horticultural Science is organised into four strands:

•      Physiology of Primary Production Organisms
•      Primary Production Systems and Their Management
•      Reproduction in Agriculture or Horticulture
•      Disciplinary Writing.

Year 13 Agricultural and Horticultural Science is organised into four strands:

•      Science and Sustainability for New Zealand Primary Production Systems
•      Innovation in Agricultural and Horticultural Science
•      Allowing for Primary Production in a Changing World
•      Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

At Year 12 Agricultural and Horticultural Science includes two constrained-choice strands:
Physiology of Primary Production Organisms and Reproduction in Agriculture or Horticulture. For
each strand, schools select either an agricultural or a horticultural context. The same context does
not need to be used across both strands. This approach provides flexibility for schools while
ensuring students engage with the intended curriculum knowledge and practices.

For the remaining Year 12 strands and for all of Year 13 content, schools teach all knowledge and
practices within the Agricultural and Horticultural Science curriculum and can determine how
learning is organised across the year. Programmes may be taught linearly or may connect learning
within and across different strands where it supports development of disciplinary knowledge and
practical capability. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary writing within subject-specific
teaching to develop students’ proficiency in scientific communication.

When designing a programme, schools are required to provide students with opportunities to
investigate production systems and management practices using practical and secondary-source
investigations. Investigation opportunities may include plant, animal, soil, environmental, and
production contexts that support evidence-based analysis and decision-making.

Pathways

Agricultural and Horticultural Science supports pathways into agriscience, horticulture, animal
science, environmental management, food and fibre production, biosecurity, viticulture, resource
management, agribusiness, primary sector innovation, and related disciplines.

Years 12–13 Biology
Students draw on biological knowledge and practices developed in earlier phases related to living
systems, inheritance, and ecological relationships. Learning builds from prior experiences to
support students to explore the interconnected nature of biological ideas across levels of
organisation, from cells and organisms to populations and ecosystems. Students strengthen their
ability to use biological knowledge, evidence, and models to explain patterns, processes, and
relationships within and between living systems.

Strands

Years 12–13 Biology is organised into four strands:

•    Biological Systems
•    Inheritance and Evolution
•    Ecology
•    Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Schools teach all knowledge and practices within the Biology curriculum. Programmes may be
taught linearly or may integrate content across strands where this supports meaningful connections
between ideas. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary writing within subject-specific teaching
to develop students’ proficiency in scientific communication.

Programmes are required to provide opportunities for students to undertake both practical and
secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively. Contexts and
investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and interests of students, their
communities, and the local environment.

Pathways

Biology leads to pathways in biology and related disciplines including biomedical science,
environmental science, biotechnology, and health sciences.

Years 12–13 Chemistry
Students are taught about the properties, structure, and composition of matter, and the physical
and chemical transformations it undergoes. They are taught how to investigate chemical systems
and processes through theoretical knowledge and practical applications. Chemistry supports
learners to engage with real-world issues and to contribute thoughtfully to solutions that affect
people and the natural world.

Strands

Years 12–13 Chemistry is organised into five strands:

•    Atomic Structure and Bonding
•    Enthalpy and Stoichiometry
•    Chemical Reactivity
•    Organic Chemistry
•    Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Schools teach all knowledge and practices within the Chemistry curriculum. Programmes may be
taught linearly or may integrate content across strands where this supports meaningful connections
between ideas. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary writing within subject-specific teaching
to develop students’ proficiency in scientific communication.

Programmes are required to provide opportunities for students to undertake both practical and
secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively. Contexts and
investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and interests of students, their
communities, and the local environment.

Pathways

Chemistry supports pathways into chemistry, biology, physics, biomedical science, medicine,
environmental science, engineering, biotechnology, health sciences, and related disciplines.

Years 12–13 Earth and Space Science
Students are taught to apply and extend scientific knowledge of Earth, atmospheric, oceanic, and
astronomical systems. They investigate how geological, climatic, oceanic, and astronomical
processes interact within interconnected systems and how scientific evidence and models are used

to explain patterns, change, and stability. Students use observations, data, models, maps, graphs,
and scientific representations to analyse phenomena, interpret evidence, and communicate
scientific explanations.

Strands

Years 12–13 Earth and Space Science is organised into five strands:

•    Earth Structures and Processes
•    The Atmosphere and Hydrosphere Interface
•    Stars and Planetary Systems
•    The Universe
•    Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Schools teach all knowledge and practices within the Earth and Space Science curriculum.
Programmes may be taught linearly or may integrate content across strands where this supports
meaningful connections between ideas. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary writing within
subject-specific teaching to develop students’ proficiency in scientific communication.

Programmes are required to provide opportunities for students to undertake both practical and
secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively. Contexts and
investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and interests of students, their
communities, and the local environment.

Pathways

Earth and Space Science supports pathways into environmental management, geology, climate
science, oceanography, planetary science, aerospace science, natural hazard management,
conservation, scientific research, and related disciplines.

Years 12–13 Physics
Students are taught to apply and extend knowledge of matter, energy, motion, forces, fields,
waves, and interactions across a wide range of scales. They investigate how physical systems
behave and interact, and how mathematical relationships, models, and evidence are used to
explain observations and make predictions. Students use measurements, graphical
representations, experiments, and mathematical analysis to investigate physical phenomena and
communicate scientific understanding.

Strands

Years 12–13 Physics is organised into six strands:

•    Foundations of Physics
•    Mechanics
•    Electricity and Magnetism

•    Waves, Oscillations, and Particles
•    Thermodynamics
•    Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Schools teach all knowledge and practices within the Physics curriculum. The Foundations of
Physics strand is designed to be integrated throughout the programme, developing the
measurement, experimental, analytical, and mathematical skills that underpin learning. The
Mechanics; Electricity and Magnetism; Waves, Oscillations, and Particles; and Thermodynamics
strands may be taught linearly or may integrate content across strands where this supports
meaningful connections between ideas. Programmes should incorporate disciplinary writing within
subject-specific teaching to develop students’ proficiency in scientific communication.

Programmes are required to provide opportunities for students to undertake both practical and
secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively. Contexts and
investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and interests of students, their
communities, and the local environment.

Pathways

Physics supports pathways into engineering, physics, astronomy, medicine, architecture,
technology, data science, electronics, energy systems, scientific research, skilled trades, and
related disciplines.


How to design a programme
•    The knowledge and practice statements within each strand are related, but teachers may
     select complementary concepts and practices from across strands to support coherence,
     depth, and meaningful connections between ideas. Disciplinary writing is most effectively
     taught when integrated across the teaching programme.
•    Science programmes should combine disciplinary knowledge, practical learning activities, and
     scientific investigations. Learning should provide opportunities for students to observe
     phenomena, gather and analyse evidence, use models and representations, test ideas,
     evaluate explanations, and communicate conclusions using scientific reasoning and evidence.
•    Investigation contexts may be adapted to reflect local environments, community priorities,
     student interests, and available resources while ensuring all intended curriculum knowledge
     and practices are taught.
•    Programmes should provide opportunities for students to engage with a range of scientific
     investigation methods, including experimentation, observation, modelling, classification,
     relationship investigations, and investigative skills including observation, secondary-source
     research.
•    Schools are required to follow the Safety and Science guidance when delivering Year 11
     Science. Further guidance on investigation design and implementation is provided in the
     Science Curriculum Support Document.

Connections to other learning areas
Science connects strongly with:

•    Mathematics and Statistics through measurement, quantitative reasoning, modelling, statistical
     analysis, and the interpretation of scientific data
•    Technology through scientific knowledge, materials, systems, energy, innovation, design, and
     problem-solving
•    Health and Physical Education through biological processes, human health, physiology,
     nutrition, disease, well-being, and evidence-based decision-making
•    Social Sciences through environmental change, sustainability, resource use, natural hazards,
     climate, and the relationships between people and natural systems
•    Geography through Earth systems, environmental processes, climate, natural hazards,
     sustainability, and human-environment interactions
•    English through disciplinary writing, communication of scientific explanations, interpretation of
     evidence, argumentation, and evaluation of scientific claims
•    The Arts through observation, representation, visual communication, design, and the
     interpretation of patterns, systems, and phenomena.
